question: Can a neural architecture modeled on a convergent term-rewriting algorithm learn recursive formula simplification, generalize to deeper out-of-distribution expressions, and share its components across several symbolic domains?

key_findings.claim: The Neural Rewriting System decomposes recursive simplification into learned selection and solving plus a deterministic executor.
key_findings.evidence: The Selector identifies reducible leaf formulas, the Solver maps a selected leaf to an atomic result or end symbol, and the Executor substitutes results into the parent expression and repeats until completion; this explicitly mirrors a term-rewriting loop.

key_findings.claim: FastNRS gains large efficiency by turning selection into token labeling and processing independent leaves in parallel.
key_findings.evidence: FastNRS uses local-receptive-field label-based positional encoding for segmentation, eliminates expensive candidate enumeration, and batches leaf solving. Reported domain models shrink modestly in parameters but reduce measured inference time from tens of minutes or hours to seconds or minutes.

key_findings.claim: Both rewriting architectures generalize to longer/deeper formulas better than the specialized transformer baseline and remain competitive with prompted frontier models on the hardest synthetic instances.
key_findings.evidence: On Logic, ListOps, Arithmetic, and Algebra, NDR drops more sharply out of distribution. GPT-4 is weaker on several tasks; o1-preview wins some intermediate OOD splits, while NRS/FastNRS equal or exceed it on the most complex reported formulas.

key_findings.claim: Systematic generalization is purchased with a hard-coded solution ontology, not learned general-purpose symbolic reasoning.
key_findings.evidence: The models assume sequence-form rewriting, atomic-value tokenization, a predefined selector/solver/executor decomposition, and task-specific tokenizers and solver vocabularies. The limitations section states that hierarchical or visual tasks and problems outside the supplied algorithmic template are not handled.

key_findings.claim: Multi-domain sharing is useful but not uniformly beneficial.
key_findings.evidence: One model handles all four domains, and NRS gains on algebra/arithmetic; FastNRS improves on ListOps and algebra but its arithmetic Solver errors increase. The error audit therefore shows both transfer and interference rather than universal compositional reuse.

method.core_idea: Embed a known convergent rewriting procedure into modular neural control flow so learned components solve local choices while deterministic execution supplies recursion.
method.mechanism: Iteratively select reducible spans, solve them, rewrite the input, and halt on an explicit token; FastNRS reframes selection as segmentation and parallelizes independent leaves.
assumptions: Tasks admit a terminating and confluent sequence-based rewrite system.
Training labels expose valid leaf selections and local reductions.
A problem-specific tokenizer and output vocabulary are available.
OOD difficulty can be varied primarily through expression depth and operand complexity.

techniques.role: Assigns learnable modules to selector and solver roles from a symbolic algorithm.
Reuses local predictions through deterministic substitution until a normal form is reached.
Makes FastNRS selection a segmentation task with restricted receptive field.
Reduces inference cost by simplifying independent selected subexpressions together.

evaluations.setting: Single-domain Logic, ListOps, Arithmetic, and Algebra with increasingly deep OOD formulas.
evaluations.result: NRS and FastNRS degrade less than NDR and are strongest on the hardest shown splits.
evaluations.baseline: Neural Data Router trained separately per task.

evaluations.setting: One multi-domain NRS or FastNRS versus GPT-4/4o prompting and o1-preview.
evaluations.metric: Exact sequence accuracy by difficulty split.
evaluations.result: The rewriting systems beat GPT-4 broadly and match or beat o1-preview at maximum reported complexity, though o1-preview wins some intermediate splits.

evaluations.setting: NRS versus FastNRS implementations across four tasks.
evaluations.metric: Parameter count and end-to-end inference time.
evaluations.result: FastNRS uses roughly 8.7M parameters on arithmetic/algebra versus roughly 9.9-10.9M for NRS and reduces reported inference from hours to under about three minutes.

limitations: Author-stated: only sequence-based rewriting tasks fit the current implementation.
Author-stated: the algorithmic blueprint and module responsibilities must be specified in advance.
Reviewer inference: direct comparison with proprietary LLMs is sensitive to prompting, model version, and unequal training/computation budgets.
Reviewer inference: 100-example accuracy splits provide limited uncertainty resolution and no independent real-world task validation.
failure_modes: Selector omits a valid leaf or chooses an overlapping/invalid span, preventing completion.
Solver produces a locally wrong atomic result whose error compounds through later rewrites.
A valid task has multiple nonconfluent rewrite paths or requires hierarchical state outside a text span.
Multi-domain gradients interfere in shared Solver representations, as observed for FastNRS arithmetic.
reusable_insights: Hard-coding recursive control flow while learning local operators can produce length generalization with small models.
Recasting combinatorial candidate selection as token labeling can dominate architectural efficiency.
Error taxonomies by selector, solver, formatting, and missing-output failures reveal transfer and interference hidden by aggregate accuracy.
open_questions: Can rewrite rules and module boundaries be induced rather than supplied?
How does performance change on unseen operators or entirely unseen rewrite systems?
Can proof certificates verify every local rewrite and turn exactness into a guaranteed property?
Does the modular advantage persist against open-weight reasoning models under matched inference compute?

competitive_landscape.title: The Neural Data Router: Adaptive Control Flow in Transformers Improves Systematic Generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: NDR learns adaptive routing inside a transformer; NRS instead fixes a selector-solver-executor rewrite loop and FastNRS labels reducible spans for parallel local execution.

competitive_landscape.title: The Devil is in the Detail: Simple Tricks Improve Systematic Generalization of Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Csordas et al. improve transformer extrapolation through architectural/training details, while this work encodes the recursive symbolic algorithm as explicit modular control flow.

competitive_landscape.title: GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: GSM-Symbolic probes fragility of general-purpose LLM reasoning under controlled perturbations; NRS targets exact synthetic formula rewriting with a task-shaped specialist architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Algorithmic Reasoning
competitive_landscape.difference: Neural Algorithmic Reasoning studies neural execution of classical algorithms, commonly over graph-structured states; this paper specializes the principle to convergent term rewriting with explicit span selection and substitution.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: FastNRS efficiently learns several convergent term-rewriting systems and systematically generalizes beyond its training distribution.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Four synthetic domains, single- and multi-domain experiments, component error audits, and measured speed/parameter comparisons support the claim in the supplied rewrite template.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest contribution is an efficient segmentation-based implementation of a known modular rewrite loop; claims about general reasoning should remain bounded to tasks whose algorithm and supervision already expose that loop.
